speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To be specific, this includes PQs filed by Members Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Louis Ng1, Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song2, Ms He Ting Ru3, Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling4, Dr Tan Wu Meng5, Dr Lim Wee Kiak6, Ms Nadia Samdin7, Mr Gan Thiam Poh8, Mr Leong Mun Wai9, Mr Alex Yam Ziming10, Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong11, Mr Vikram Nair12, Mr Yip Hon Weng13 and Miss Rachel Ong14.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As the details of the site clearance at the Kranji site have been shared publicly by JTC at a press conference on 22 February, I will focus my response today on: one, environmental considerations in the planning process; two, on-going investigations into the incident at the Kranji site; and three, steps that we plan to take to strengthen our processes, including the environmental impact assessment (EIA) framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA’s) Planning Act, development proposals require planning permission from URA before they are allowed to proceed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As part of this process, every development proposal goes through a thorough screening process, which reviews not only its potential environmental impact, but also other aspects such as its impact on traffic, public health and heritage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Developments projects that: one, are near sensitive areas such as Nature Reserves, Nature Areas and other areas with significant biodiversity; or two, which are in marine and coastal areas; or three, which have potential trans-boundary impact, are subject to greater scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The developers of such projects will be required to undergo an in-depth consultation process with relevant technical agencies, namely NParks, National Environment Agency (NEA), the Maritime Port Authority (MPA) and the Singapore Food Agency (SFA).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Depending on the context of the site, the scope of the project works, and its potential impact on the environment, more detailed studies may be required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This can be an Environmental Baseline Study (EBS), or in some cases, a more detailed Environmental Impact Study (EIS), which sets out the environmental baseline, expected impact and mitigation measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The studies enable agencies to better assess the possible environmental impact of the development plans and the adequacy of the proposed mitigation measures, to guide the planning and potential development of the site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, NEA assesses the potential for noise, water or air pollution, MPA assesses impacts on navigation and SFA on sea-based farms, NParks assesses impacts on terrestrial and marine biodiversity, covering both flora and fauna.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We adopt this calibrated approach across all development projects, whether they are for industrial or other uses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While developers can call tenders for works while the environmental studies are on-going, activities on site can only proceed when the developer has received the necessary approvals from relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This applies for both private and public projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the Parks and Trees Act, the felling of any tree more than one metre in girth either on vacant land or in Tree Conservation areas can only proceed with the Commissioner's approval.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks will require a tree survey, in order to assess the potential impact of the tree felling plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If NParks assesses that conducting a further environmental baseline, or other forms of study, is not required, it may allow for some types of works to begin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, NParks may require mitigation measures, such as the installation of hoarding or an Environmental Monitoring and Management Programme (EMMP) to be in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For past incidents of tree felling without prior approval, NParks had conducted investigations and penalties ensued.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The environmental impact of such incidents varies depending on the site context and the extent of works undertaken.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Planning permission for the project to go ahead is only granted after a project has met the requirements imposed by the respective regulatory agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include completing necessary detailed technical studies, such as environmental and traffic impact assessments, as well as putting in place mitigating measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many Members have asked for updates on the investigations and the possible penalties on the site clearance at Kranji site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We therefore cannot go into more detail at this point, and we ask that Members not speculate further.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After investigations are complete, NParks will refer the case to the Public Prosecutor for directions, before sharing the findings with the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are penalties for breaches of the Parks and Trees Act and the Wildlife Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members have also asked if the site clearance at the Kranji Road/Kranji Close site had affected the fauna baseline study.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All clearance works onsite are currently suspended, while the study is underway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The results of the study will be made public when ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Thereafter, JTC will engage relevant stakeholders on the findings, including the measures to enhance the greenery and connectivity of the site and its surrounding environs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The study findings will be used to design measures such as enhanced habitats, buffers and connectivity for wildlife.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Now, I move on to the third part of the presentation which is on steps to strengthen processes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members have asked how we will seek to prevent such incidents from happening again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Agencies involved in site clearance projects are conducting checks to ensure that their project supervision and implementation processes are in order.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In our discussions with the nature community last year, we had identified several other ways to further strengthen the EIA process beyond what we had just rolled out in October.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will develop a more comprehensive picture of the islandwide eco-system and connectivity, so that we can better consider how the specific sites connect to our nature cores, buffers and corridors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will do this in a science-based manner, on an islandwide scale, and we will conduct baseline studies for specific sites to understand their ecological profile and role in ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members of the nature community will be invited to join us in this upstream work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The findings from these studies will add to the data and connectivity models that NParks has built up over the years, and help guide Government in carrying out longer term planning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, we have been reviewing whether it would be better to centralise the management of EIA consultants, instead of having individual developers or agencies manage their own.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Separately, we will explore how we can make better use of technology to strengthen project management.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The land that we got back included the 24-km railway line, from North all the way South to Tanjong Pagar Railway Station, as well as adjacent parcels of land at various points along the track.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These parcels of land were used by the railway for storage, for housing and for other purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We struck a careful balance between conservation and development in our land use planning for the land that was returned, as follows.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, by conserving the railway station building in Tanjong Pagar and the old Bukit Timah Railway Station, or BTRS, as part of our heritage and history.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And thirdly, by zoning the adjacent land parcels along the railway tracks, including the Kranji site, for development, to meet our people's needs for homes, jobs and amenities and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we struck balance in three ways, and if Members may recall in the last Parliamentary Question (PQ) over Ulu Pandan Forest, as I sought to provide the broad outline of how we steward our land to meet various needs, including that for nature, for housing, for jobs and so on and so forth, we include a strategy of big moves – for example, Greater Southern Waterfront, Paya Lebar air base relocation and, of course, this KTM line that we brought back, including the land parcels adjacent, along the way – was one of those moves as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the Kranji site, as Minister Chan Chun Sing had explained earlier, it comprised mostly scrubland scattered with trees when it was returned to Singapore in 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Until the detailed plans were finalised and works begun, the site was left vacant, with vegetation and trees allowed to grow to provide green cover until the time of development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Non-native Albizia trees sprouted in recent years – and biologists would know that Albizia trees grow at a very quick rate, they self-sow and they grow as fast as four to five metres a year and can mature in as fast as five years or less – and in Singapore's hot and humid climate, progressively dominated the site within a few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, sites that have been cleared and with intention for some form of development, even as they are left fallow and bare, we allowed vegetation, green cover, so we enjoy that for the few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have explained in this House recently, we adopt a science-based approach to identify which areas of significant biodiversity to conserve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, the Mandai Mangrove and Mudflat, just further north of the Kranji site, was once a fishing village.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It had initially been planned for industrial use, for factories.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Yet, after careful study through biodiversity surveys and ecological modelling, we decided to keep it as a Nature Park given its high ecological value, both domestically as well as internationally as part of a flyway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Agencies, therefore, had to forego development plans for the area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For sites to be developed, we seek to preserve and integrate natural elements within the development where possible, to facilitate ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think this incident has certainly shocked and disappointed many of us when we learn of it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Also, I can imagine that our staff at NParks feel the same; I know they take great pains to strengthen and improve the green cover and green space for the country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have three supplementary questions for Minister Chan.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Seah, if you can keep it to two supplementary questions, then more Members can ask.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, my first supplementary question is, is there a schedule for the frequency of site visits by the project manager?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Is it meant to be daily, weekly, or monthly?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Second supplementary question, the internal investigation by JTC, I would like to ask will this be complemented with an investigation by an external party?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: And my third supplementary question is, it has been mentioned that stern warning has been issued to the contractor.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Stern warning appears to me to be quite light.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: What does "stern warning" mean and what are the consequences?

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Whether that schedule has been adhered to, is the subject of an on-going investigation at this point in time and I will not further comment on this.

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, on the nature of the investigations, as I have laid out on Monday, there are the internal NParks and JTC investigations as to whether the current processes have been followed.

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I expect the respective agencies will want to do a thorough review to see whether the processes have been followed.

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Joseph will have access to both the views from the public sector, the people sector and also the private sector.

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The penalties for those are laid out in the respective Acts.

speaker: The Ministry for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, it does not mean that the stern warning is the end of all there is to be.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister for National Development and one supplementary question for the Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the Minister for National Development, I would like to ask the Minister whether he thinks that it is now time to consider codifying Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA) and other similar assessments like the Environmental Baseline Study (EBS) into our legislative framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That means to have a law that codifies all these assessments, quite akin to what they have in the UK, where it prescribes when the EIA must be done, and when it does not have to be done, the legislation will state that it is because it is provided for in a differently scheduled provision under a separate area of law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Related to this, under such a proposed framework, I would like to ask the Minister for National Development whether or not, in the proposed review that he is looking into, to consider a more holistic approach in assessment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the moment, it is different types of assessment that we are doing – EBS, EIA, and the assessment that Minister Chan has mentioned because of the different conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, I wonder if we can have a more holistic approach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And I say this because, for example, in this case, both Ministers mentioned about scrubland, that this Kranji woodlands being scrubland —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Dennis Tan, if you could keep your supplementary questions short.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is a number of Members who would like to ask supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Currently, it provides for our biodiversity – there is wildlife, there is floral and fauna.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But eventually, it can also develop into something even better over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, if we have a holistic approach that can look into land of such a nature, it is in-between, it may not be secondary forest, but nonetheless, it is important biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Next, I would like to ask the Minister for Trade and Industry whether the Minister can confirm that Huationg has been paid for the land clearance that it carried out in December last year and January this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will address the questions he has asked about the EIA framework, and then, my colleague Minister Chan will respond.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first is whether we want or need to codify the Environmental Impact Assessment framework into legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think we need to see what the framework is in place, currently, today, as augmented by recent developments, both in June last year and October last year; as well as the plans we have going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We look at EIA framework as a whole; and legislation is a tool as are other levers such as guidelines, incentives, processes, standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They all are different tools with which we use to ensure that the framework is holistic, rigorous and comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said previously, no development, public or private, may take place without planning permission.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said earlier, there is not only a masterplanning process in which multiple agencies representing the diversity of needs of Singaporeans, both present and future, but also representing the different constituencies and causes and concerns out there, come together regularly as part of the masterplanning process to look at our land use needs, including sites that we may need for connectivity, for biodiversity, for nature, for recreation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But also, when development plans are surfaced, way in advance of even the first works beginning onsite, there is a screening process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, URA acts as a gateway; the Planning Act and related planning legislation are the legislative tools which URA uses to provide that gatekeeping role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And a variety of technical agencies will then scrutinise the plans specifically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Each site will have its own variances, its own habitat, its own set of issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of it could be traffic, some of it could be hydrology, some of it could be water quality, some of it could be issues of sedimentation, some about noise, some about biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where nature and biodiversity are concerned, NParks together with the professionals and scientists and arborists and horticulturalists and conservationists, with the support of the nature community whom we consult regularly, we will look at those sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will look at those sites for which a development plan is put forward for approval, and then, make an assessment and screen it – notwithstanding the upstream masterplanning phase when plans arrive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The different agencies, depending on the specific context of the site, impose or require the necessary consultations, studies, which are then pegged onto that planning approval legislative framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This kind of approach allows for greater dexterity, greater responsiveness to the site in question.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, there are other legislation involving, say, the pollution of waterways, pollution of water bodies, rivers, earth streams, so and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, there is a legislative framework and they all come together, not just codified, and frozen in time, but responsive, allowing gatekeeping roles, allowing agencies to come in to making impositions, to impose studies, to then look at those studies and impose the EMMP and other plants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the approach is holistic having said that last October last year, we sought to strengthen the capability of the sector, strengthen the capability that we have locally, strengthen both the understanding of developing agencies as well as EIA consultants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our nature community tells us that actually what needs to be done is we need to bootstrap, up the standards and ensure consistency in our biodiversity impact assessment capability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And hence, a very comprehensive approach in our new BIA guidelines which were launched in October last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I am not quite sure how you can codify something like the BIA guidelines which will be used across different agencies, because it is very comprehensive from a scientific basis, looking at different habitats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, when there is a mangrove habitat, whether it is intertidal, whether it is whether it is a secondary forest, whether it is scrubland, whether it is a mature forest, whether you look at the benthic habitats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All these are specifically set out in very detailed guidelines, put together by conservationists and in deep consultation with our nature community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, when development is about to begin and is in progress, there are powers under the Parks and Trees Act, powers to require a tree and flora survey, for which then you can decide whether to grant approval for the clearance of trees or the salvage or the conservation intitule of trees onsite that are of significance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As well as under the Wildlife Act, the imposition of EMMPs, as well as fauna surveys.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I also request that the Ministers keep their responses as succinct as possible?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The first is in terms of the timing of the announcement by JTC on 16 February, can the Minister provide an explanation on that timeline?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The discovery of the erroneous clearance was on 13 January and it would seem the announcement came after a member of the public – a private citizen – first shared about this on social media.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The second question is to just pay recognition to the fact that this land is ultimately for agri-technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a general rule as to when we make investigations public, a few considerations will have to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, will it affect the course of the investigations, will it prejudice the course of the investigations?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the nature of the incident and which aspect of it will be of public interest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our focus from January to February, within JTC, was to make sure that they can conduct the investigation thoroughly and fairly, without prejudice to the parties concerned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we can all understand that once things come out to the public, certain evidence or certain investigations might be prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is why we have not made public earlier the investigations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But when there was public interest in this, we were also careful to make sure that we come out quickly with the facts that we have established, so that the public does not need to speculate, so that we can proceed with the investigations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, we will complete the EMMP study, and then, we will consult the necessary stakeholders, and then, we will try to progress the project as originally planned in order to deliver, not just the economic benefits, the jobs, the food resilience, but also to deliver as part of the masterplan, the environmental enhancement in the area that will allow us to enjoy the place, live in the place, work in the place and play in the place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many agencies are involved in land clearance works involving greenery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes LTA, HDB, PUB, JTC, SLA and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of the follow-ups, will the Government consider appointing a lead agency to oversee and overall coordinate land clearance activities, such that we can minimise the possibility of such an incident from happening again?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At this point in time, I want to qualify.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we say strengthen the process, we mean to make it better, we mean to streamline it, and it does not necessarily mean that we must add on more processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I may seek your indulgence, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I grew up in the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And in the SAF, once in a while, sometimes, accidents happen.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And very often when accidents happen, we ask ourselves how we can do better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And very often, sometimes, we will come to a quick conclusion that we need more supervision.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have grown up learning that, that may not necessarily be the best solution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because when more parties get involved, ultimately, who is responsible?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If a soldier did not do his job well, we ask whether there were factors that affected his concentration, whether his training was adequate or whether there were other complicating factors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that, indeed, we should be careful that in trying to improve the processes and streamline the processes, we do not unnecessarily add on processes that might either diffuse the responsibility or make project coordination even more difficult going forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As we know, the contractors currently working on the ground are already facing various kinds of challenges from adhering to regulations to the challenges posed by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we should all try to come together to see how we can streamline the processes to improve the processes so that everyone is clear about their lines of accountability.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I may just add, there will be many diverse interests in a complex project like this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are developmental interests, there are contractors' interests, there are environmental groups' interests.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And in all that we do, we seek to find a balance amongst all these interests, so that as much of the interest can be accommodated as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is how we will move forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is not either one or the other, it is not binary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is always about working together to find the best way forward, so that we can achieve multiple objectives from environmental protection to development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I have this question for the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Have there been plots of land that was earmarked earlier for industrial or housing development, that is under the masterplan, and was actually traded off in the interest of nature and also environmental protection over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You know that as part of the concept plan or now what we call the long-term planning process, we identify the broad strategies for Singapore and therefore, flow through the land use requirements into the masterplan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Agencies come together to look at the different sites, look at the needs that they have for housing, recreation, healthcare, nature, conservation, for heritage, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And then, they work out the masterplan, which is then exhibited and publicly consulted on, including by specific stakeholders and interest groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But having said that, over the years, this is not a static process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is an iterative process, a dynamic one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because our land use needs, population needs, our natural spaces also evolve and change, and therefore we have to be flexible and nimble and agile, and continuously relook at our masterplan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, as I have said in my presentation earlier, there have been sites which have been zoned for other uses, but which, after discussion between agencies, after the use of scientific approaches, have had their plans changed and agencies forgo their initial intentions for that land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, where the Kranji site is, it was once railway land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The parcel was made complete by agreed re-routing of the rail corridor, but then, JTC then decided to put it back in again, because they felt that it was important to have that within an Agri-food Innovation Park, in consultation with NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But just further north, is the Mandai Mangrove and Mudflat, which is a key habitat; it is ecologically linked to Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve and also important as part of the East-Asian Australasian Flyway for migratory birds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Likewise, a little further east would be Sungei Khatib Bongsu.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Once, it was for prawn farming and fish farming as well as housing, kampong and some human use; subsequently, kept fallow for future development, specifically housing; and those plans were forgone after we evaluated the site and decided to keep it for nature areas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One for the Minister for Trade and Industry and one for Minister for National Development.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Trade and Industry, was this erroneously cleared 4.5 hectares of land, would it have been eventually cleared anyway and if so, when would that have been done?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And for the Minister for National Development, the Minister, I believe, said that the developers can start planning works while environmental studies are on-going but they have to wait for approval before proceeding.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, if detailed requirements for developments are drawn out and multimillion-dollar tenders are issued before the studies are completed, is there a risk that the clearance of natural vegetation becoming a fait accompli by the time the environmental studies are completed?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If all the necessary environmental considerations had been addressed, then the plan will be executed in full, as per what is shown in the slide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member makes a very good point.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But ultimately, the developer has to make a call whether they wish to proceed to call those tenders, and if so, then they run the risk of having to make major adjustments along the way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just two quick questions for Minister Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, I think Minister mentioned about the BIA guidelines earlier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, I do hope we can codify the current EIA framework into law because I think that will send a strong signal that we take the protection of forests seriously here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I recognise the Member's longstanding advocacy for the legislative codification of the EIA process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said previously, there is legislative gatekeeping and legislative empowerment in the entire process, but this is not just a legal process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is an environmental process, a conservation process, a scientific process and it requires flexibility depending on the habitats and on the ecology of the area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And therefore, I think what we have today is an evolving system with recent enhancements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let us work on that and continue to study how we can improve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hope through this process for developing agencies, including public developing agencies, to have a consistent baseline standard in carrying out these processes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let us see how it is put into process and then decide what next steps to take.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The site in question is in my constituency and I have observed first-hand the change to the site on many walks with my residents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By equal measure, my residents also look forward to the transformation of Sungei Kadut to bring more jobs and residential opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have two quick supplementary questions – one to the Minister for National Development; it is more factual.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It relates to part of my question on how many such unauthorised clearances have occurred in the last 12 months and what were the actions taken to them?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second is for the Minister-in-charge of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As mentioned by a number of Members, many public officers are involved in any large scale and complex project, and often resulting in cross responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How does the Minister-in-charge of the Public Service plan to look into the processes and into this incident as a learning point, so that such unauthorised actions do not occur again?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Minister shared earlier that Permanent Secretary Joseph Leong will be looking into this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister share if there are specific areas that the Permanent Secretary will be directed to look at so that we can improve on processes?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What would Permanent Secretary Joseph Leong do and then a second part is how do we approach this issue going forward?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first, as I have mentioned in my response to Mr Yip Hon Weng's question, indeed, there are many parties involved in a complex project like this, including many parties within the Public Service and of course the private contractors, the consultants and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If people are not up to the task, we have to ask ourselves how do we equip them, train them to do their job better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, at the end of the day, at the heart of it all, no matter how many rules we have for all the agencies, for all the parties involved, ultimately, at the heart of it, we need people with the right values.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I say this particularly for the Public Service – people with the right values who are conscious of their duties, determined to execute it well and constantly find areas to improve when the need arises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have every confidence that I have such a Public Service, in service of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we look at how the Public Service has done over the last one year through the COVID-19 pandemic, everyone not only doing what they are supposed to do but going above and beyond their call of duty when called upon to do well for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have confidence that they will look at this thoroughly, learn the lessons and improve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because when I speak to the officers in JTC and NParks and when I look at them in the eye, I know.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I see in their eyes the fire in their belly that they want to put this right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am sure that even if I have not tasked them to do so, they themselves would want to get it right and improve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the kind of Public Service that has brought Singapore to where it is today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the kind of Public Service that we can entrust our future together.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the order of the day.
